{{poli-term-stub}}
'''Shashoku''' (社稷) is the collective term for the '''sha''' (a ceremonial platform enshrining the tutelary deity of the land) and the '''jiki''' (a ceremonial platform enshrining the deity of grains).
Originally, these were the objects of ritual in the ceremonies of the feudal lords during the Zhou period; however, after the imperial period of the {{ill|Empire|en|Empire|WD=Q48349|lt=Empire|1=Empire}} of the Qin and Han dynasties, along with the {{ill|Temple of Heaven|en|Temple of Heaven|WD=Q125445|lt=Tiantan|1=Temple of Heaven}}, {{ill|Temple of Earth|en|Temple of Earth|WD=Q615178|lt=Ditian|1=Temple of Earth}}, and {{ill|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|en|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|WD=Q10948212|lt=Confucian royal ancestral shrine|1=Confucian royal ancestral shrine}}, the shashoku came to play a central role in the state rituals of China<ref name="ブリタニカ">[https://kotobank.jp/word/%E7%A4%BE%E7%A8%B7-75970]{{ill|Britannica International Encyclopedia|ja|ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 小項目事典|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Britannica International Encyclopedia|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}</ref>, and by extension, it came to denote the very "【State】" or national polity.
It is related to the ancient spring and autumn equinox rituals, and its festival day, the {{ill|Shari|ja|社日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shari|1=Q11019584|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11019584}}, often coincides with the equinoctial period ({{ill|Higan|en|Higan|WD=Q866977|lt=Higan|1=Higan}}) of spring and autumn. In Taiwan and Vietnam ({{ill|Vietnam|ja|越南|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Vietnam|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ベトナム|1=Vietnam|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q881}}), the term "sha" evolved from meaning the land deity to refer to administrative districts. In Japan, the original meaning of the word used to name a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto Shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} is thought to have been a small shrine enshrining a tutelary land deity. From the notion of "sha" came the idea of a community association (a group of parishioners), which eventually led to the coining of modern words such as "kaisha" (company).
== === History == In ancient China during the feudal society of the Zhou period, the land and the crops harvested from it were considered the foundation of the feudal states, and each village enshrined both the land deity (sha) and the grain deity ({{ill|Five Grains|en|Five Grains|WD=Q1191138|lt=Five Grains|1=Five Grains}}). After the fall of the Zhou and the rise of the {{ill|Empire|en|Empire|WD=Q48349|lt=Empire|1=Empire}} of the Qin and Han dynasties, the Son of Heaven (the Emperor) began to conduct state rituals centered on the shashoku, and over time shashoku came to signify the state and the national polity itself.
When a new state arose, altars for shashoku and ancestral temples ({{ill|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|en|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|WD=Q10948212|lt=Confucian royal ancestral shrine|1=Confucian royal ancestral shrine}}) were established. The capital of the empire was traditionally arranged so that the ancestral shrine of the founders (called the Taizu, enshrined in the ancestral temple) was placed on the left, and the land deity (shashoku) on the right<ref>{{Cite book |language=ja |author=小柳司気太 |year=1923 |title=道教概論 |publisher=世界文庫刊行会 |pages=P.10 |note={{ill|Rites of Zhou|en|Rites of Zhou|WD=Q1367984|lt=Zhou Li|1=Rites of Zhou}} and {{ill|Kaogongji|en|Kaogongji|WD=Q13640977|lt=Kang Gong Ji|1=Kaogongji}} mention this arrangement}}</ref>. Many extant shashoku altars in China, Vietnam, and Korea follow this form, which is said to have existed since the Zhou period.
Within Confucianism, it was mandated not only to protect the ancestral temples of the current dynasty but also those of past dynasties. This was to demonstrate that the reigning dynasty possessed virtue ({{ill|De (Chinese)|en|De (Chinese)|WD=Q1179705|lt=Virtue|1=De (Chinese)}}) comparable to that of previous dynasties and to attest to the legitimacy ({{ill|Dynastic cycle|en|Dynastic cycle|WD=Q5319145|lt=Yi-Xing Revolution|1=Dynastic cycle}}) that replaced a previous, declining dynasty.
The desecration of the ancestral temples and tombs of past emperors was recognized as a sign that the current regime (or the virtue of its dynasty) was in a state of instability. Consequently, under the legal codes ({{ill|Traditional Chinese law|en|Traditional Chinese law|WD=Q4380197|lt=Ritsuryō|1=Traditional Chinese law}}), no matter which dynasty it was, the desecration of the ancestral temples and tombs of previous emperors was harshly punished as an offense nearly as serious as treason ({{ill|Mouhan|ja|謀反|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mouhan|1=plotting rebellion|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11632156}} or {{ill|Mōdaigyaku|ja|謀大逆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mōdaigyaku|1=plotting sedition|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q18339539}}).<ref>{{Cite web |title=唐律疏议/卷第十七 - 维基文库，自由的图书馆 |url=https://zh.wikisource.org/zh-hans/%E5%94%90%E5%BE%8B%E7%96%8F%E8%AD%B0/%E5%8D%B7%E7%AC%AC%E5%8D%81%E4%B8%83 |website=zh.wikisource.org |access-date=2023-03-10 |language=zh-Hans}}</ref>
== = The Shashoku Altar == {{Referencesの明記| section = 1| date = 2020th year 6月}}
In the modern era, within the {{ill|Ming dynasty|en|Ming dynasty|WD=Q9903|lt=Ming|1=Ming dynasty}} Empire, the {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing|1=Qing dynasty}} Empire, the {{ill|Nguyen Dynasty|ja|大南帝国|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nguyen Dynasty|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Vietnam, and the {{ill|Korean Empire|en|Korean Empire|WD=Q28233|lt=Daehan Empire|1=Korean Empire}}, the shashoku altar was composed of two parts: the sha altar (dedicated to the land deity) and the jiki altar (dedicated to the grain deity). On top of the shashoku altar were spread five types of colored earth, brought as offerings from the frontiers in the directions specified below (the center being yellow, the east blue, the south red, the west white, and the north black). According to the theories of Yin-Yang and Wuxing Theory, these five colors represent all things under heaven – in other words, all land – encapsulated in the maxim “In all the world, there is no land that is not the property of the Emperor” (indicating that the entire world is under the Emperor’s dominion, as per {{ill|Sinocentrism|en|Sinocentrism|WD=Q1370788|lt=Sinocentrism|1=Sinocentrism}}).
In Japan, during the Taishō period, figures such as {{ill|Shibusawa Eiichi|en|Shibusawa Eiichi|WD=Q704995|lt=Shibusawa Eiichi|1=Shibusawa Eiichi}} in his work ''Bushi to Sanban'' (1916) referred to the national shashoku in expressions like “[https://messe.nikkei.co.jp/rt/column/bible/60508.html The Shashoku of 300 Years of the Tokugawa]”, and {{ill|Gondō Narikiyo|ja|権藤成卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gondō Narikiyo|1=Seikyō Gondō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2903172}} advocated the ideal of a shashoku-type feudal system, promoting the notion of a "shashoku state" as a community of mutual assistance and coexistence. From ancient to modern times, the term shashoku was accepted as referring to the national polity of the feudal states of the Zhou period. In Japan, there are no examples of the national shashoku altar being established or the Emperor conducting state rituals of shashoku (although there are instances, such as that of {{ill|Fujiwara no Kanezane|en|Fujiwara no Kanezane|WD=Q710214|lt=Kujō Kanezane|1=Fujiwara no Kanezane}}, where the term shashoku was used in the sense of the state or national polity); rather, the only example is the private shrine of the Tokugawa family, where a {{ill|Shennōbyō|ja|神農廟|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shennōbyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} was set up within the {{ill|Yushima Seidō|en|Yushima Seidō|WD=Q1760591|lt=Yushima Seidō|1=Yushima Seidō}}. Furthermore, the concept of a day for enshrining the "sha" in the Chinese calendar – the {{ill|Shari|ja|社日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shari|1=Q11019584|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11019584}} (or "Inu no Hi" [the Dog Day], which falls just before or after the equinoxes on approximately March 20 and September 23, and is also known as Harusha and Akusha) – was also adopted in Japan in a form that coincides with the equinoctial period. Since the spring and autumn equinoxes are holidays based on the solar calendar, the corresponding spring and autumn shari become movable feasts in the traditional lunisolar calendar. In Reiwa 3 (2021), the spring shari fell on the old calendar date 2/03 (corresponding to March 15 on the Gregorian calendar), and the autumn shari on the old calendar date 8/17 (corresponding to Thursday, September 23 – the day of the autumn equinox).
== = Shashoku in China == The Beijing Shashoku Altar of the {{ill|Ming dynasty|en|Ming dynasty|WD=Q9903|lt=Ming|1=Ming dynasty}} and {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing|1=Qing dynasty}} Empires is located within modern-day {{ill|Beijing|en|Beijing|WD=Q956|lt=Beijing|1=Beijing}}, to the south of the {{ill|Forbidden City|en|Forbidden City|WD=Q80290|lt=Forbidden City|1=Forbidden City}} and west of the {{ill|Tiananmen|en|Tiananmen|WD=Q83973|lt=Tiananmen|1=Tiananmen}}, in what is now {{ill|Zhongshan Park|en|Zhongshan Park|WD=Q2622640|lt=Zhongshan Park|1=Zhongshan Park}}. Originally established using a temple that had existed since the Tang dynasty, it is said to have been founded in 1420 by {{ill|Hongwu Emperor|en|Hongwu Emperor|WD=Q9957|lt=Zhu Yuanzhang|1=Hongwu Emperor}}, the founder of the Ming dynasty. The name "Zhongshan Park" derives from the fact that the casket of {{ill|Sun Yat-sen|en|Sun Yat-sen|WD=Q8573|lt=Sun Yat-sen|1=Sun Yat-sen}} (also known by his courtesy name, Zhongshan, who died in 1925), the "Father of the Chinese Revolution", is enshrined in the {{ill|Zhongshan Hall|en|Zhongshan Hall|WD=Q6145247|lt=Zhongshan Hall|1=Zhongshan Hall}} within the park. Originally, the Zhongshan Hall served as the worship hall, constructed in the Ming dynasty; it was the venue where the Ming and Qing emperors conducted ceremonies to avoid inclement weather while enshrining the deities. However, after Sun Yat-sen’s casket was interred there, the hall was renamed Zhongshan Hall in 1928, and the entire shashoku altar complex was renamed Zhongshan Park. Traditionally, the Chinese rulers were believed to receive the Mandate of Heaven here. Zhongshan Park still houses numerous ancient cypress trees, some said to be over a thousand years old, which are regarded as connecting heaven and earth. The current Chinese leader, {{ill|Xi Jinping|en|Xi Jinping|WD=Q15031|lt=Xi Jinping|1=Xi Jinping}}, who serves as General Secretary of the {{ill|General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party|en|General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party|WD=Q849418|lt=Communist Party of China|1=General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party}} and President of the {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=People's Republic of China|1=China}}, is also perceived as paying close attention to the Beijing Shashoku Altar as part of his role as China’s ruler.
== = Shashoku in Korea and North Korea == At {{ill|Gyeongbokgung|en|Gyeongbokgung|WD=Q482485|lt=Gyeongbokgung Palace|1=Gyeongbokgung}}, an ancestral temple is located on the east side and a shashoku altar ({{ill|Sashikdan|ja|社稷壇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sashikdan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) on the west side, both of which have been designated as important cultural properties in South Korea. In addition, place names such as Sashik-dong (社稷洞) and Sashik-ro (社稷路) in Seoul bear testimony to this heritage. Every year, the city of Seoul holds the [https://m.korea.net/japanese/NewsFocus/History/view?articleId=140938&page=1]{{ill|Seoul Shashoku Festival|ja|ソウル社稷大祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seoul Shashoku Festival|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Autumn Shashoku Festival).
In Chinese literature, the government of North Korea under the {{ill|Workers' Party of Korea|en|Workers' Party of Korea|WD=Q49623|lt=Workers’ Party of Korea|1=Workers' Party of Korea}} has been referred to as the “Four Carriages of the Korean Shashoku Organization.” These four carriages specifically denote the {{ill|Supreme People's Assembly|en|Supreme People's Assembly|WD=Q714698|lt=Supreme People's Assembly|1=Supreme People's Assembly}}, its {{ill|Standing Committee|ja|最高人民会議常任委員会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Standing Committee|1=Standing Committee of the Supreme People's Assembly|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11515680}}, the {{ill|State Affairs Commission|ja|国務委員会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/State Affairs Commission|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 朝鮮民主主義人民共和国国務委員会|1=State Affairs Commission of North Korea|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q25263528}} (formerly the National Defense Commission), and the {{ill|Cabinet (government)|en|Cabinet (government)|WD=Q640506|lt=Cabinet|1=Cabinet (government)}} of North Korea.
== = Shashoku in Vietnam == {{Referencesの明記| section = 1| date = 2020th year 6月}} According to {{ill|Ngô Sĩ Liên|en|Ngô Sĩ Liên|WD=Q716585|lt=Ngô Thời Lân|1=Ngô Sĩ Liên}}’s ''{{ill|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|en|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|WD=Q855899|lt=Đại Việt Sử Ký Toàn Thư|1=Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư}}'', the beginning of shashoku rituals in Vietnam can be traced back to the founding of the Hoa Lu Shashoku Altar by Ding Bùlǐng, the former emperor of the Ding dynasty of Đại Cổ Quế Quốc, in the first year of the 【Kai Bao】 era (968) during the reign of {{ill|Song Taizu|ja|宋太祖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Song Taizu|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 趙匡胤|1=Emperor Taizu of Song|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7471}}. Since the Ding dynasty, shashoku rituals in Vietnam have been regarded as major national ceremonies. During the {{ill|Nguyễn dynasty|en|Nguyễn dynasty|WD=Q6500483|lt=Nguyễn Dynasty|1=Nguyễn dynasty}}, not only was the shashoku altar established at the national level, but altars were also set up in each province alongside the {{ill|Temple of Confucius|en|Temple of Confucius|WD=Q618618|lt=Confucius Temple|1=Temple of Confucius}} (also known as the Wen or Holy Temple). These local shashoku rituals continue to be observed today, such as in the case of the "[https://btgcp.gov.vn/tin-trong-nuoc/Le_hoi_den_Xa_Tac___cot_moc_van_hoa_noi_bien_ai-postrm06axpx.html Quang Ninh Province, Mong Cai City Shashoku Festival]" (as reported by the Vietnamese Government’s Religious Affairs Division).
Regarding the national shashoku altar in Vietnam, according to records in {{ill|Lê Quý Đôn|ja|黎貴惇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lê Quý Đôn|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}’s ''{{ill|Minh Vân Tiểu Lục|ja|見聞小録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minh Vân Tiểu Lục|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'', the Shenglun Shashoku Altar (the Hanoi Shashoku Altar) was established by Lê Thánh Tông (also known as {{ill|Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja|阮世祖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}/Nguyễn Phúc Ảnh, also called Jialong Di [Zha Long Di]) during the reign of the Hong De period of the {{ill|Lê dynasty|en|Lê dynasty|WD=Q10800789|lt=Lê Dynasty|1=Lê dynasty}}. After Lê Thánh Tông’s death, a series of royal struggles and internecine conflicts ensued (Lê Dynasty → Mạc Dynasty → Lê-Mạc Wars → Zheng-Nguyễn Wars → Zheng-Xishan Wars → {{ill|Tây Sơn dynasty|en|Tây Sơn dynasty|WD=Q1034173|lt=Seoshan Dynasty|1=Tây Sơn dynasty}} → Nguyễn-Xishan Wars → {{ill|Nguyễn dynasty|en|Nguyễn dynasty|WD=Q6500483|lt=Nguyễn Dynasty|1=Nguyễn dynasty}}). The Hanoi Shashoku Altar (consisting of the sha altar and the jiki altar) was completely destroyed soon after Lê Quý Đôn’s account (after the abdication of Emperor Lê Mín, around 1788), and its original location was lost; however, in November 2006, the remains of the sha altar were discovered during road construction in Hanoi. Consequently, place names such as Phường Xã Đàn and Đường Xã Đàn have been derived from it. In addition, the "Fuh Chun Shashoku Altar" in Hue, as recorded in the first volume of the corrected edition of the ''{{ill|Đại Nam Thực Lục Chính Biên|ja|大南寔録正編|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Đại Nam Thực Lục Chính Biên|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'', was established in the fourth year of the Jia Long era (1805–1806) by Emperor {{ill|Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja|阮世祖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Đại Nam (the Nguyễn Dynasty). Even under French colonial rule, it was not destroyed; a portion still remains in Hue City (the capital of Thừa Thiên–Huế Province) in the area known as Phường Thuận Hóa, and since 2008 the provincial government has been holding the [https://thuathienhue.gov.vn/vi-vn/Thong-tin-du-dia-chi/tid/Le-te-Xa-Tac/newsid/710FF67B-C749-4E5F-AA2D-A73F00AE0887/cid/11920A02-33B3-4D47-BBF1-EA00ED61C66D Hue Shashoku Festival] (Autumn Shashoku Festival) there. The shashoku rituals of Thừa Thiên–Huế Province, like those in Quang Ninh Province, are now recognized by the state and the Communist Party (via the Government Religious Affairs Division) as official local ceremonies.
In Vietnamese celestial charts, the portion of the zodiac corresponding to the {{ill|Scorpio (astrology)|en|Scorpio (astrology)|WD=Q134398|lt=Scorpius|1=Scorpio (astrology)}} – namely, the {{ill|Room (Chinese constellation)|en|Room (Chinese constellation)|WD=Q1145870|lt=Fangxiu|1=Room (Chinese constellation)}} (consisting of stars such as those in the π Scorpii group) – is envisioned as the crown, while the {{ill|Heart (Chinese constellation)|en|Heart (Chinese constellation)|WD=Q1145909|lt=Xin Xiu|1=Heart (Chinese constellation)}} (comprising stars such as {{ill|Antares|en|Antares|WD=Q12166|lt=Antares|1=Antares}}) is seen as a rounded back; together, these asterisms are identified with {{ill|Shennong|en|Shennong|WD=Q313336|lt=Shennong|1=Shennong}} (see [https://www.noron.vn/post/than-nong-co-phai-chom-sao-bo-cap-efsjh7gst6y Thần Nông]), and are revered as the shashoku deity (the grain deity). This Vietnamese constellation corresponds to the {{ill|Azure Dragon|ja|青龍|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Azure Dragon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 青竜|1=Azure Dragon|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q515882}} of Chinese star lore. According to the Vietnamese myth recorded in the ''{{ill|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|en|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|WD=Q855899|lt=Đại Việt Sử Ký Toàn Thư|1=Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư}}'', Hun Vương (the first king of the Bunlang State of the Hong family, also identified with {{ill|Kinh Dương Vương|en|Kinh Dương Vương|WD=Q1140378|lt=Jingyangwang|1=Kinh Dương Vương}}/King Jin-Son), was a descendant (or grandson in the third generation) of the first Shennong of the Flame Emperor (【Di Shinian】), and was depicted with a dragon body.
The Vietnamese revolutionary leader {{ill|Ho Chi Minh (disambiguation)|en|Ho Chi Minh (disambiguation)|WD=Q611752|lt=Ho Chi Minh|1=Ho Chi Minh (disambiguation)}} (Hu Chi Minh) had contacts with the elder {{ill|Sun Yat-sen|en|Sun Yat-sen|WD=Q8573|lt=Sun Yat-sen|1=Sun Yat-sen}} during his stay in Guangzhou (1924–1925) and revered him as a great revolutionary; however, likely due to the fact that the hall enshrining Sun Yat-sen (the {{ill|Zhongshan Hall|en|Zhongshan Hall|WD=Q6145247|lt=Zhongshan Hall|1=Zhongshan Hall}}) was located within the Beijing Shashoku Altar (the Chinese shashoku), which symbolized the Chinese state, Vietnamese people avoided using the name "Zhongshan" and instead referred to Sun Yat-sen respectfully as "Mr. Sun Wen" or "Mr. Sun Yat-sen."

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ar:تربة وحبوب]][[en:Soil and grain]][[fa:زمین و غلات]][[id:Tanah dan sereal]][[nl:Sheji]][[zh-classical:社稷]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[fa:زمین و غلات]][[id:Tanah dan sereal]][[nl:Sheji]][[zh-classical:社稷]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[fa:زمین و غلات]][[id:Tanah dan sereal]][[nl:Sheji]][[zh-classical:社稷]] [[ja:社稷]] [[ko:사직 (역사)]] [[zh:社稷]] [[ar:تربة وحبوب]] [[en:Soil and grain]] [[ja:社稷]] [[ko:사직 (역사)]] [[zh:社稷]] [[ar:تربة وحبوب]] [[en:Soil and grain]] [[ja:社稷]] [[ko:사직 (역사)]] [[zh:社稷]] {{Infobox deity}}{{Short description|Historic term for the state in East Asia}} __NOTOC__ {{infobox chinese |title= |pic= |piccap= |name1= |c={{linktext|社稷}} |p=shèjì |w=she-chi |kanji={{linktext|社稷}} |revhep=shashoku |hangul=사직 |rr=sajik |qn=xã tắc |chuhan={{linktext|社稷}} }} '''Soil and grain''' was a common {{ill|Chinese culture|en|Chinese culture|WD=Q645917|lt=Chinese|1=Chinese culture}} political term in the [[:en:East Asian cultural sphere|Sinosphere]] for the {{ill|State (polity)|en|State (polity)|WD=Q7275|lt=state|1=State (polity)}}. [[:en:Shejitan|Shejitan]], the altars of soil and grain, were constructed alongside ancestral altars. Chinese monarchs of the {{ill|Ming dynasty|en|Ming dynasty|WD=Q9903|lt=Ming|1=Ming dynasty}} and {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing|1=Qing dynasty}} dynasties performed ceremonies of soil and grain to affirm their sovereignty at the {{ill|Beijing Shejitan|en|Beijing Shejitan|WD=Q1361047|lt=Beijing Shejitan|1=Beijing Shejitan}}.
During the Chinese {{ill|Warring States period|en|Warring States period|WD=Q185063|lt=Warring States period|1=Warring States period}}, ministers defied their rulers by claiming a greater loyalty to the "soil and grain".<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=zhpLJgHZMTQC&pg=PA164 Envisioning eternal empire: Chinese political thought of the Warring States era]</ref>
A similar concept to ''sheji'' is that of the earth deities [[:en:Tu Di Gong|Tudi]] and {{ill|Houtu|en|Houtu|WD=Q3235126|lt=Houtu|1=Houtu}}.<ref>[[:en:C.K. Yang (sociologist)|Yang, C. K.]] ''Religion in Chinese Society : A Study of Contemporary Social Functions of Religion and Some of Their Historical Factors'' (1967 [1961]). Berkeley and Los Angeles: University of California Press. page 97</ref> It is also linked to {{ill|Sheshen|en|Sheshen|WD=Q15904843|lt=Sheshen|1=Sheshen}} or deities which are sometimes directly called soil (社)
{{ill|Houtu|en|Houtu|WD=Q3235126|lt=Houtu|1=Houtu}} is the overlord of all the {{ill|Tudigong|en|Tudigong|WD=Q2670522|lt=Tudigongs|1=Tudigong}} ("Lord of Local Land"), [[Soil and grain|Sheji]] ("the State"), [[:en:Shanshen|Shan Shen]] ("God of Mountains"), {{ill|City God (China)|en|City God (China)|WD=Q702182|lt=City Gods|1=City God (China)}} ("God of Local City"), and [[:en:landlord gods|landlord gods]] world wide.
==In other cultures== Korean monarchs of the {{ill|Joseon|en|Joseon|WD=Q28179|lt=Joseon dynasty|1=Joseon}} did so at the {{ill|Sajikdan|en|Sajikdan|WD=Q491000|lt=Seoul Sajikdan|1=Sajikdan}}.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=8qvY8pxVxcwC&pg=PA371 A comparative study of thirty city states]</ref> It has also been rendered "gods of soil and grain" in English, owing to its associations of prayer and supernatural possibilities.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=zqdHRAY4hAUC&pg=PA138 Hymes: Way and Byway (Google Books)]</ref>
== {{Anchor|Altar}}Sheji altar == Sheji altars (社稷坛) are altars dedicated to soil and grain. {{ill|Beijing Shejitan|en|Beijing Shejitan|WD=Q1361047|lt=Beijing Shejitan|1=Beijing Shejitan}} is the most famous example.

'''Shashoku''' (社稷) is the collective term for the '''sha''' (a ceremonial platform enshrining the tutelary deity of the land) and the '''jiki''' (a ceremonial platform enshrining the deity of grains).
Originally, these were the objects of ritual in the ceremonies of the feudal lords during the Zhou period; however, after the imperial period of the {{ill|Empire|en|Empire|WD=Q48349|lt=Empire|1=Empire}} of the Qin and Han dynasties, along with the {{ill|Temple of Heaven|en|Temple of Heaven|WD=Q125445|lt=Tiantan|1=Temple of Heaven}}, {{ill|Temple of Earth|en|Temple of Earth|WD=Q615178|lt=Ditian|1=Temple of Earth}}, and {{ill|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|en|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|WD=Q10948212|lt=Confucian royal ancestral shrine|1=Confucian royal ancestral shrine}}, the shashoku came to play a central role in the state rituals of China<ref name="ブリタニカ">[https://kotobank.jp/word/%E7%A4%BE%E7%A8%B7-75970]{{ill|Britannica International Encyclopedia|ja|ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 小項目事典|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Britannica International Encyclopedia|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}</ref>, and by extension, it came to denote the very "【State】" or national polity.
It is related to the ancient spring and autumn equinox rituals, and its festival day, the {{ill|Shari|ja|社日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shari|1=Q11019584|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11019584}}, often coincides with the equinoctial period ({{ill|Higan|en|Higan|WD=Q866977|lt=Higan|1=Higan}}) of spring and autumn. In Taiwan and Vietnam ({{ill|Vietnam|ja|越南|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Vietnam|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ベトナム|1=Vietnam|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q881}}), the term "sha" evolved from meaning the land deity to refer to administrative districts. In Japan, the original meaning of the word used to name a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto Shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} is thought to have been a small shrine enshrining a tutelary land deity. From the notion of "sha" came the idea of a community association (a group of parishioners), which eventually led to the coining of modern words such as "kaisha" (company).
== === History == In ancient China during the feudal society of the Zhou period, the land and the crops harvested from it were considered the foundation of the feudal states, and each village enshrined both the land deity (sha) and the grain deity ({{ill|Five Grains|en|Five Grains|WD=Q1191138|lt=Five Grains|1=Five Grains}}). After the fall of the Zhou and the rise of the {{ill|Empire|en|Empire|WD=Q48349|lt=Empire|1=Empire}} of the Qin and Han dynasties, the Son of Heaven (the Emperor) began to conduct state rituals centered on the shashoku, and over time shashoku came to signify the state and the national polity itself.
When a new state arose, altars for shashoku and ancestral temples ({{ill|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|en|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|WD=Q10948212|lt=Confucian royal ancestral shrine|1=Confucian royal ancestral shrine}}) were established. The capital of the empire was traditionally arranged so that the ancestral shrine of the founders (called the Taizu, enshrined in the ancestral temple) was placed on the left, and the land deity (shashoku) on the right<ref>{{Cite book |language=ja |author=小柳司気太 |year=1923 |title=道教概論 |publisher=世界文庫刊行会 |pages=P.10 |note={{ill|Rites of Zhou|en|Rites of Zhou|WD=Q1367984|lt=Zhou Li|1=Rites of Zhou}} and {{ill|Kaogongji|en|Kaogongji|WD=Q13640977|lt=Kang Gong Ji|1=Kaogongji}} mention this arrangement}}</ref>. Many extant shashoku altars in China, Vietnam, and Korea follow this form, which is said to have existed since the Zhou period.
Within Confucianism, it was mandated not only to protect the ancestral temples of the current dynasty but also those of past dynasties. This was to demonstrate that the reigning dynasty possessed virtue ({{ill|De (Chinese)|en|De (Chinese)|WD=Q1179705|lt=Virtue|1=De (Chinese)}}) comparable to that of previous dynasties and to attest to the legitimacy ({{ill|Dynastic cycle|en|Dynastic cycle|WD=Q5319145|lt=Yi-Xing Revolution|1=Dynastic cycle}}) that replaced a previous, declining dynasty.
The desecration of the ancestral temples and tombs of past emperors was recognized as a sign that the current regime (or the virtue of its dynasty) was in a state of instability. Consequently, under the legal codes ({{ill|Traditional Chinese law|en|Traditional Chinese law|WD=Q4380197|lt=Ritsuryō|1=Traditional Chinese law}}), no matter which dynasty it was, the desecration of the ancestral temples and tombs of previous emperors was harshly punished as an offense nearly as serious as treason ({{ill|Mouhan|ja|謀反|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mouhan|1=plotting rebellion|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11632156}} or {{ill|Mōdaigyaku|ja|謀大逆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mōdaigyaku|1=plotting sedition|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q18339539}}).<ref>{{Cite web |title=唐律疏议/卷第十七 - 维基文库，自由的图书馆 |url=https://zh.wikisource.org/zh-hans/%E5%94%90%E5%BE%8B%E7%96%8F%E8%AD%B0/%E5%8D%B7%E7%AC%AC%E5%8D%81%E4%B8%83 |website=zh.wikisource.org |access-date=2023-03-10 |language=zh-Hans}}</ref>
== = The Shashoku Altar == {{Referencesの明記| section = 1| date = 2020th year 6月}}
In the modern era, within the {{ill|Ming dynasty|en|Ming dynasty|WD=Q9903|lt=Ming|1=Ming dynasty}} Empire, the {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing|1=Qing dynasty}} Empire, the {{ill|Nguyen Dynasty|ja|大南帝国|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nguyen Dynasty|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Vietnam, and the {{ill|Korean Empire|en|Korean Empire|WD=Q28233|lt=Daehan Empire|1=Korean Empire}}, the shashoku altar was composed of two parts: the sha altar (dedicated to the land deity) and the jiki altar (dedicated to the grain deity). On top of the shashoku altar were spread five types of colored earth, brought as offerings from the frontiers in the directions specified below (the center being yellow, the east blue, the south red, the west white, and the north black). According to the theories of Yin-Yang and Wuxing Theory, these five colors represent all things under heaven – in other words, all land – encapsulated in the maxim “In all the world, there is no land that is not the property of the Emperor” (indicating that the entire world is under the Emperor’s dominion, as per {{ill|Sinocentrism|en|Sinocentrism|WD=Q1370788|lt=Sinocentrism|1=Sinocentrism}}).
In Japan, during the Taishō period, figures such as {{ill|Shibusawa Eiichi|en|Shibusawa Eiichi|WD=Q704995|lt=Shibusawa Eiichi|1=Shibusawa Eiichi}} in his work ''Bushi to Sanban'' (1916) referred to the national shashoku in expressions like “[https://messe.nikkei.co.jp/rt/column/bible/60508.html The Shashoku of 300 Years of the Tokugawa]”, and {{ill|Gondō Narikiyo|ja|権藤成卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gondō Narikiyo|1=Seikyō Gondō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2903172}} advocated the ideal of a shashoku-type feudal system, promoting the notion of a "shashoku state" as a community of mutual assistance and coexistence. From ancient to modern times, the term shashoku was accepted as referring to the national polity of the feudal states of the Zhou period. In Japan, there are no examples of the national shashoku altar being established or the Emperor conducting state rituals of shashoku (although there are instances, such as that of {{ill|Fujiwara no Kanezane|en|Fujiwara no Kanezane|WD=Q710214|lt=Kujō Kanezane|1=Fujiwara no Kanezane}}, where the term shashoku was used in the sense of the state or national polity); rather, the only example is the private shrine of the Tokugawa family, where a {{ill|Shennōbyō|ja|神農廟|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shennōbyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} was set up within the {{ill|Yushima Seidō|en|Yushima Seidō|WD=Q1760591|lt=Yushima Seidō|1=Yushima Seidō}}. Furthermore, the concept of a day for enshrining the "sha" in the Chinese calendar – the {{ill|Shari|ja|社日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shari|1=Q11019584|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11019584}} (or "Inu no Hi" [the Dog Day], which falls just before or after the equinoxes on approximately March 20 and September 23, and is also known as Harusha and Akusha) – was also adopted in Japan in a form that coincides with the equinoctial period. Since the spring and autumn equinoxes are holidays based on the solar calendar, the corresponding spring and autumn shari become movable feasts in the traditional lunisolar calendar. In Reiwa 3 (2021), the spring shari fell on the old calendar date 2/03 (corresponding to March 15 on the Gregorian calendar), and the autumn shari on the old calendar date 8/17 (corresponding to Thursday, September 23 – the day of the autumn equinox).
== = Shashoku in China == The Beijing Shashoku Altar of the {{ill|Ming dynasty|en|Ming dynasty|WD=Q9903|lt=Ming|1=Ming dynasty}} and {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing|1=Qing dynasty}} Empires is located within modern-day {{ill|Beijing|en|Beijing|WD=Q956|lt=Beijing|1=Beijing}}, to the south of the {{ill|Forbidden City|en|Forbidden City|WD=Q80290|lt=Forbidden City|1=Forbidden City}} and west of the {{ill|Tiananmen|en|Tiananmen|WD=Q83973|lt=Tiananmen|1=Tiananmen}}, in what is now {{ill|Zhongshan Park|en|Zhongshan Park|WD=Q2622640|lt=Zhongshan Park|1=Zhongshan Park}}. Originally established using a temple that had existed since the Tang dynasty, it is said to have been founded in 1420 by {{ill|Hongwu Emperor|en|Hongwu Emperor|WD=Q9957|lt=Zhu Yuanzhang|1=Hongwu Emperor}}, the founder of the Ming dynasty. The name "Zhongshan Park" derives from the fact that the casket of {{ill|Sun Yat-sen|en|Sun Yat-sen|WD=Q8573|lt=Sun Yat-sen|1=Sun Yat-sen}} (also known by his courtesy name, Zhongshan, who died in 1925), the "Father of the Chinese Revolution", is enshrined in the {{ill|Zhongshan Hall|en|Zhongshan Hall|WD=Q6145247|lt=Zhongshan Hall|1=Zhongshan Hall}} within the park. Originally, the Zhongshan Hall served as the worship hall, constructed in the Ming dynasty; it was the venue where the Ming and Qing emperors conducted ceremonies to avoid inclement weather while enshrining the deities. However, after Sun Yat-sen’s casket was interred there, the hall was renamed Zhongshan Hall in 1928, and the entire shashoku altar complex was renamed Zhongshan Park. Traditionally, the Chinese rulers were believed to receive the Mandate of Heaven here. Zhongshan Park still houses numerous ancient cypress trees, some said to be over a thousand years old, which are regarded as connecting heaven and earth. The current Chinese leader, {{ill|Xi Jinping|en|Xi Jinping|WD=Q15031|lt=Xi Jinping|1=Xi Jinping}}, who serves as General Secretary of the {{ill|General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party|en|General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party|WD=Q849418|lt=Communist Party of China|1=General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party}} and President of the {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=People's Republic of China|1=China}}, is also perceived as paying close attention to the Beijing Shashoku Altar as part of his role as China’s ruler.
== = Shashoku in Korea and North Korea == At {{ill|Gyeongbokgung|en|Gyeongbokgung|WD=Q482485|lt=Gyeongbokgung Palace|1=Gyeongbokgung}}, an ancestral temple is located on the east side and a shashoku altar ({{ill|Sashikdan|ja|社稷壇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sashikdan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) on the west side, both of which have been designated as important cultural properties in South Korea. In addition, place names such as Sashik-dong (社稷洞) and Sashik-ro (社稷路) in Seoul bear testimony to this heritage. Every year, the city of Seoul holds the [https://m.korea.net/japanese/NewsFocus/History/view?articleId=140938&page=1]{{ill|Seoul Shashoku Festival|ja|ソウル社稷大祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seoul Shashoku Festival|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Autumn Shashoku Festival).
In Chinese literature, the government of North Korea under the {{ill|Workers' Party of Korea|en|Workers' Party of Korea|WD=Q49623|lt=Workers’ Party of Korea|1=Workers' Party of Korea}} has been referred to as the “Four Carriages of the Korean Shashoku Organization.” These four carriages specifically denote the {{ill|Supreme People's Assembly|en|Supreme People's Assembly|WD=Q714698|lt=Supreme People's Assembly|1=Supreme People's Assembly}}, its {{ill|Standing Committee|ja|最高人民会議常任委員会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Standing Committee|1=Standing Committee of the Supreme People's Assembly|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11515680}}, the {{ill|State Affairs Commission|ja|国務委員会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/State Affairs Commission|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 朝鮮民主主義人民共和国国務委員会|1=State Affairs Commission of North Korea|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q25263528}} (formerly the National Defense Commission), and the {{ill|Cabinet (government)|en|Cabinet (government)|WD=Q640506|lt=Cabinet|1=Cabinet (government)}} of North Korea.
== = Shashoku in Vietnam == {{Referencesの明記| section = 1| date = 2020th year 6月}} According to {{ill|Ngô Sĩ Liên|en|Ngô Sĩ Liên|WD=Q716585|lt=Ngô Thời Lân|1=Ngô Sĩ Liên}}’s ''{{ill|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|en|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|WD=Q855899|lt=Đại Việt Sử Ký Toàn Thư|1=Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư}}'', the beginning of shashoku rituals in Vietnam can be traced back to the founding of the Hoa Lu Shashoku Altar by Ding Bùlǐng, the former emperor of the Ding dynasty of Đại Cổ Quế Quốc, in the first year of the 【Kai Bao】 era (968) during the reign of {{ill|Song Taizu|ja|宋太祖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Song Taizu|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 趙匡胤|1=Emperor Taizu of Song|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7471}}. Since the Ding dynasty, shashoku rituals in Vietnam have been regarded as major national ceremonies. During the {{ill|Nguyễn dynasty|en|Nguyễn dynasty|WD=Q6500483|lt=Nguyễn Dynasty|1=Nguyễn dynasty}}, not only was the shashoku altar established at the national level, but altars were also set up in each province alongside the {{ill|Temple of Confucius|en|Temple of Confucius|WD=Q618618|lt=Confucius Temple|1=Temple of Confucius}} (also known as the Wen or Holy Temple). These local shashoku rituals continue to be observed today, such as in the case of the "[https://btgcp.gov.vn/tin-trong-nuoc/Le_hoi_den_Xa_Tac___cot_moc_van_hoa_noi_bien_ai-postrm06axpx.html Quang Ninh Province, Mong Cai City Shashoku Festival]" (as reported by the Vietnamese Government’s Religious Affairs Division).
Regarding the national shashoku altar in Vietnam, according to records in {{ill|Lê Quý Đôn|ja|黎貴惇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lê Quý Đôn|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}’s ''{{ill|Minh Vân Tiểu Lục|ja|見聞小録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minh Vân Tiểu Lục|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'', the Shenglun Shashoku Altar (the Hanoi Shashoku Altar) was established by Lê Thánh Tông (also known as {{ill|Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja|阮世祖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}/Nguyễn Phúc Ảnh, also called Jialong Di [Zha Long Di]) during the reign of the Hong De period of the {{ill|Lê dynasty|en|Lê dynasty|WD=Q10800789|lt=Lê Dynasty|1=Lê dynasty}}. After Lê Thánh Tông’s death, a series of royal struggles and internecine conflicts ensued (Lê Dynasty → Mạc Dynasty → Lê-Mạc Wars → Zheng-Nguyễn Wars → Zheng-Xishan Wars → {{ill|Tây Sơn dynasty|en|Tây Sơn dynasty|WD=Q1034173|lt=Seoshan Dynasty|1=Tây Sơn dynasty}} → Nguyễn-Xishan Wars → {{ill|Nguyễn dynasty|en|Nguyễn dynasty|WD=Q6500483|lt=Nguyễn Dynasty|1=Nguyễn dynasty}}). The Hanoi Shashoku Altar (consisting of the sha altar and the jiki altar) was completely destroyed soon after Lê Quý Đôn’s account (after the abdication of Emperor Lê Mín, around 1788), and its original location was lost; however, in November 2006, the remains of the sha altar were discovered during road construction in Hanoi. Consequently, place names such as Phường Xã Đàn and Đường Xã Đàn have been derived from it. In addition, the "Fuh Chun Shashoku Altar" in Hue, as recorded in the first volume of the corrected edition of the ''{{ill|Đại Nam Thực Lục Chính Biên|ja|大南寔録正編|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Đại Nam Thực Lục Chính Biên|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'', was established in the fourth year of the Jia Long era (1805–1806) by Emperor {{ill|Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja|阮世祖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Đại Nam (the Nguyễn Dynasty). Even under French colonial rule, it was not destroyed; a portion still remains in Hue City (the capital of Thừa Thiên–Huế Province) in the area known as Phường Thuận Hóa, and since 2008 the provincial government has been holding the [https://thuathienhue.gov.vn/vi-vn/Thong-tin-du-dia-chi/tid/Le-te-Xa-Tac/newsid/710FF67B-C749-4E5F-AA2D-A73F00AE0887/cid/11920A02-33B3-4D47-BBF1-EA00ED61C66D Hue Shashoku Festival] (Autumn Shashoku Festival) there. The shashoku rituals of Thừa Thiên–Huế Province, like those in Quang Ninh Province, are now recognized by the state and the Communist Party (via the Government Religious Affairs Division) as official local ceremonies.
In Vietnamese celestial charts, the portion of the zodiac corresponding to the {{ill|Scorpio (astrology)|en|Scorpio (astrology)|WD=Q134398|lt=Scorpius|1=Scorpio (astrology)}} – namely, the {{ill|Room (Chinese constellation)|en|Room (Chinese constellation)|WD=Q1145870|lt=Fangxiu|1=Room (Chinese constellation)}} (consisting of stars such as those in the π Scorpii group) – is envisioned as the crown, while the {{ill|Heart (Chinese constellation)|en|Heart (Chinese constellation)|WD=Q1145909|lt=Xin Xiu|1=Heart (Chinese constellation)}} (comprising stars such as {{ill|Antares|en|Antares|WD=Q12166|lt=Antares|1=Antares}}) is seen as a rounded back; together, these asterisms are identified with {{ill|Shennong|en|Shennong|WD=Q313336|lt=Shennong|1=Shennong}} (see [https://www.noron.vn/post/than-nong-co-phai-chom-sao-bo-cap-efsjh7gst6y Thần Nông]), and are revered as the shashoku deity (the grain deity). This Vietnamese constellation corresponds to the {{ill|Azure Dragon|ja|青龍|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Azure Dragon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 青竜|1=Azure Dragon|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q515882}} of Chinese star lore. According to the Vietnamese myth recorded in the ''{{ill|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|en|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|WD=Q855899|lt=Đại Việt Sử Ký Toàn Thư|1=Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư}}'', Hun Vương (the first king of the Bunlang State of the Hong family, also identified with {{ill|Kinh Dương Vương|en|Kinh Dương Vương|WD=Q1140378|lt=Jingyangwang|1=Kinh Dương Vương}}/King Jin-Son), was a descendant (or grandson in the third generation) of the first Shennong of the Flame Emperor (【Di Shinian】), and was depicted with a dragon body.
The Vietnamese revolutionary leader {{ill|Ho Chi Minh (disambiguation)|en|Ho Chi Minh (disambiguation)|WD=Q611752|lt=Ho Chi Minh|1=Ho Chi Minh (disambiguation)}} (Hu Chi Minh) had contacts with the elder {{ill|Sun Yat-sen|en|Sun Yat-sen|WD=Q8573|lt=Sun Yat-sen|1=Sun Yat-sen}} during his stay in Guangzhou (1924–1925) and revered him as a great revolutionary; however, likely due to the fact that the hall enshrining Sun Yat-sen (the {{ill|Zhongshan Hall|en|Zhongshan Hall|WD=Q6145247|lt=Zhongshan Hall|1=Zhongshan Hall}}) was located within the Beijing Shashoku Altar (the Chinese shashoku), which symbolized the Chinese state, Vietnamese people avoided using the name "Zhongshan" and instead referred to Sun Yat-sen respectfully as "Mr. Sun Wen" or "Mr. Sun Yat-sen."

[[:en:Shejitan|Shejitan]], the altars of soil and grain, were constructed alongside ancestral altars. Chinese monarchs of the {{ill|Ming dynasty|en|Ming dynasty|WD=Q9903|lt=Ming|1=Ming dynasty}} and {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing|1=Qing dynasty}} dynasties performed ceremonies of soil and grain to affirm their sovereignty at the {{ill|Beijing Shejitan|en|Beijing Shejitan|WD=Q1361047|lt=Beijing Shejitan|1=Beijing Shejitan}}.
During the Chinese {{ill|Warring States period|en|Warring States period|WD=Q185063|lt=Warring States period|1=Warring States period}}, ministers defied their rulers by claiming a greater loyalty to the "soil and grain".<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=zhpLJgHZMTQC&pg=PA164 Envisioning eternal empire: Chinese political thought of the Warring States era]</ref>
A similar concept to ''sheji'' is that of the earth deities [[:en:Tu Di Gong|Tudi]] and {{ill|Houtu|en|Houtu|WD=Q3235126|lt=Houtu|1=Houtu}}.<ref>[[:en:C.K. Yang (sociologist)|Yang, C. K.]] ''Religion in Chinese Society : A Study of Contemporary Social Functions of Religion and Some of Their Historical Factors'' (1967 [1961]). Berkeley and Los Angeles: University of California Press. page 97</ref> It is also linked to {{ill|Sheshen|en|Sheshen|WD=Q15904843|lt=Sheshen|1=Sheshen}} or deities which are sometimes directly called soil (社)
{{ill|Houtu|en|Houtu|WD=Q3235126|lt=Houtu|1=Houtu}} is the overlord of all the {{ill|Tudigong|en|Tudigong|WD=Q2670522|lt=Tudigongs|1=Tudigong}} ("Lord of Local Land"), [[Soil and grain|Sheji]] ("the State"), [[:en:Shanshen|Shan Shen]] ("God of Mountains"), {{ill|City God (China)|en|City God (China)|WD=Q702182|lt=City Gods|1=City God (China)}} ("God of Local City"), and [[:en:landlord gods|landlord gods]] world wide.
==In other cultures== Korean monarchs of the {{ill|Joseon|en|Joseon|WD=Q28179|lt=Joseon dynasty|1=Joseon}} did so at the {{ill|Sajikdan|en|Sajikdan|WD=Q491000|lt=Seoul Sajikdan|1=Sajikdan}}.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=8qvY8pxVxcwC&pg=PA371 A comparative study of thirty city states]</ref> It has also been rendered "gods of soil and grain" in English, owing to its associations of prayer and supernatural possibilities.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=zqdHRAY4hAUC&pg=PA138 Hymes: Way and Byway (Google Books)]</ref>
== {{Anchor|Altar}}Sheji altar == Sheji altars (社稷坛) are altars dedicated to soil and grain. {{ill|Beijing Shejitan|en|Beijing Shejitan|WD=Q1361047|lt=Beijing Shejitan|1=Beijing Shejitan}} is the most famous example.

'''Shashoku''' (社稷) is the collective term for the '''sha''' (a ceremonial platform enshrining the tutelary deity of the land) and the '''jiki''' (a ceremonial platform enshrining the deity of grains).
Originally, these were the objects of ritual in the ceremonies of the feudal lords during the Zhou period; however, after the imperial period of the {{ill|Empire|en|Empire|WD=Q48349|lt=Empire|1=Empire}} of the Qin and Han dynasties, along with the {{ill|Temple of Heaven|en|Temple of Heaven|WD=Q125445|lt=Tiantan|1=Temple of Heaven}}, {{ill|Temple of Earth|en|Temple of Earth|WD=Q615178|lt=Ditian|1=Temple of Earth}}, and {{ill|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|en|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|WD=Q10948212|lt=Confucian royal ancestral shrine|1=Confucian royal ancestral shrine}}, the shashoku came to play a central role in the state rituals of China<ref name="ブリタニカ">[https://kotobank.jp/word/%E7%A4%BE%E7%A8%B7-75970]{{ill|Britannica International Encyclopedia|ja|ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 小項目事典|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Britannica International Encyclopedia|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}</ref>, and by extension, it came to denote the very "【State】" or national polity.
It is related to the ancient spring and autumn equinox rituals, and its festival day, the {{ill|Shari|ja|社日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shari|1=Q11019584|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11019584}}, often coincides with the equinoctial period ({{ill|Higan|en|Higan|WD=Q866977|lt=Higan|1=Higan}}) of spring and autumn. In Taiwan and Vietnam ({{ill|Vietnam|ja|越南|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Vietnam|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ベトナム|1=Vietnam|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q881}}), the term "sha" evolved from meaning the land deity to refer to administrative districts. In Japan, the original meaning of the word used to name a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto Shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} is thought to have been a small shrine enshrining a tutelary land deity. From the notion of "sha" came the idea of a community association (a group of parishioners), which eventually led to the coining of modern words such as "kaisha" (company).
== === History == In ancient China during the feudal society of the Zhou period, the land and the crops harvested from it were considered the foundation of the feudal states, and each village enshrined both the land deity (sha) and the grain deity ({{ill|Five Grains|en|Five Grains|WD=Q1191138|lt=Five Grains|1=Five Grains}}). After the fall of the Zhou and the rise of the {{ill|Empire|en|Empire|WD=Q48349|lt=Empire|1=Empire}} of the Qin and Han dynasties, the Son of Heaven (the Emperor) began to conduct state rituals centered on the shashoku, and over time shashoku came to signify the state and the national polity itself.
When a new state arose, altars for shashoku and ancestral temples ({{ill|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|en|Confucian royal ancestral shrine|WD=Q10948212|lt=Confucian royal ancestral shrine|1=Confucian royal ancestral shrine}}) were established. The capital of the empire was traditionally arranged so that the ancestral shrine of the founders (called the Taizu, enshrined in the ancestral temple) was placed on the left, and the land deity (shashoku) on the right<ref>{{Cite book |language=ja |author=小柳司気太 |year=1923 |title=道教概論 |publisher=世界文庫刊行会 |pages=P.10 |note={{ill|Rites of Zhou|en|Rites of Zhou|WD=Q1367984|lt=Zhou Li|1=Rites of Zhou}} and {{ill|Kaogongji|en|Kaogongji|WD=Q13640977|lt=Kang Gong Ji|1=Kaogongji}} mention this arrangement}}</ref>. Many extant shashoku altars in China, Vietnam, and Korea follow this form, which is said to have existed since the Zhou period.
Within Confucianism, it was mandated not only to protect the ancestral temples of the current dynasty but also those of past dynasties. This was to demonstrate that the reigning dynasty possessed virtue ({{ill|De (Chinese)|en|De (Chinese)|WD=Q1179705|lt=Virtue|1=De (Chinese)}}) comparable to that of previous dynasties and to attest to the legitimacy ({{ill|Dynastic cycle|en|Dynastic cycle|WD=Q5319145|lt=Yi-Xing Revolution|1=Dynastic cycle}}) that replaced a previous, declining dynasty.
The desecration of the ancestral temples and tombs of past emperors was recognized as a sign that the current regime (or the virtue of its dynasty) was in a state of instability. Consequently, under the legal codes ({{ill|Traditional Chinese law|en|Traditional Chinese law|WD=Q4380197|lt=Ritsuryō|1=Traditional Chinese law}}), no matter which dynasty it was, the desecration of the ancestral temples and tombs of previous emperors was harshly punished as an offense nearly as serious as treason ({{ill|Mouhan|ja|謀反|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mouhan|1=plotting rebellion|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11632156}} or {{ill|Mōdaigyaku|ja|謀大逆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mōdaigyaku|1=plotting sedition|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q18339539}}).<ref>{{Cite web |title=唐律疏议/卷第十七 - 维基文库，自由的图书馆 |url=https://zh.wikisource.org/zh-hans/%E5%94%90%E5%BE%8B%E7%96%8F%E8%AD%B0/%E5%8D%B7%E7%AC%AC%E5%8D%81%E4%B8%83 |website=zh.wikisource.org |access-date=2023-03-10 |language=zh-Hans}}</ref>
== = The Shashoku Altar == {{Referencesの明記| section = 1| date = 2020th year 6月}}
In the modern era, within the {{ill|Ming dynasty|en|Ming dynasty|WD=Q9903|lt=Ming|1=Ming dynasty}} Empire, the {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing|1=Qing dynasty}} Empire, the {{ill|Nguyen Dynasty|ja|大南帝国|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nguyen Dynasty|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Vietnam, and the {{ill|Korean Empire|en|Korean Empire|WD=Q28233|lt=Daehan Empire|1=Korean Empire}}, the shashoku altar was composed of two parts: the sha altar (dedicated to the land deity) and the jiki altar (dedicated to the grain deity). On top of the shashoku altar were spread five types of colored earth, brought as offerings from the frontiers in the directions specified below (the center being yellow, the east blue, the south red, the west white, and the north black). According to the theories of Yin-Yang and Wuxing Theory, these five colors represent all things under heaven – in other words, all land – encapsulated in the maxim “In all the world, there is no land that is not the property of the Emperor” (indicating that the entire world is under the Emperor’s dominion, as per {{ill|Sinocentrism|en|Sinocentrism|WD=Q1370788|lt=Sinocentrism|1=Sinocentrism}}).
In Japan, during the Taishō period, figures such as {{ill|Shibusawa Eiichi|en|Shibusawa Eiichi|WD=Q704995|lt=Shibusawa Eiichi|1=Shibusawa Eiichi}} in his work ''Bushi to Sanban'' (1916) referred to the national shashoku in expressions like “[https://messe.nikkei.co.jp/rt/column/bible/60508.html The Shashoku of 300 Years of the Tokugawa]”, and {{ill|Gondō Narikiyo|ja|権藤成卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gondō Narikiyo|1=Seikyō Gondō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2903172}} advocated the ideal of a shashoku-type feudal system, promoting the notion of a "shashoku state" as a community of mutual assistance and coexistence. From ancient to modern times, the term shashoku was accepted as referring to the national polity of the feudal states of the Zhou period. In Japan, there are no examples of the national shashoku altar being established or the Emperor conducting state rituals of shashoku (although there are instances, such as that of {{ill|Fujiwara no Kanezane|en|Fujiwara no Kanezane|WD=Q710214|lt=Kujō Kanezane|1=Fujiwara no Kanezane}}, where the term shashoku was used in the sense of the state or national polity); rather, the only example is the private shrine of the Tokugawa family, where a {{ill|Shennōbyō|ja|神農廟|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shennōbyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} was set up within the {{ill|Yushima Seidō|en|Yushima Seidō|WD=Q1760591|lt=Yushima Seidō|1=Yushima Seidō}}. Furthermore, the concept of a day for enshrining the "sha" in the Chinese calendar – the {{ill|Shari|ja|社日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shari|1=Q11019584|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11019584}} (or "Inu no Hi" [the Dog Day], which falls just before or after the equinoxes on approximately March 20 and September 23, and is also known as Harusha and Akusha) – was also adopted in Japan in a form that coincides with the equinoctial period. Since the spring and autumn equinoxes are holidays based on the solar calendar, the corresponding spring and autumn shari become movable feasts in the traditional lunisolar calendar. In Reiwa 3 (2021), the spring shari fell on the old calendar date 2/03 (corresponding to March 15 on the Gregorian calendar), and the autumn shari on the old calendar date 8/17 (corresponding to Thursday, September 23 – the day of the autumn equinox).
== = Shashoku in China == The Beijing Shashoku Altar of the {{ill|Ming dynasty|en|Ming dynasty|WD=Q9903|lt=Ming|1=Ming dynasty}} and {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing|1=Qing dynasty}} Empires is located within modern-day {{ill|Beijing|en|Beijing|WD=Q956|lt=Beijing|1=Beijing}}, to the south of the {{ill|Forbidden City|en|Forbidden City|WD=Q80290|lt=Forbidden City|1=Forbidden City}} and west of the {{ill|Tiananmen|en|Tiananmen|WD=Q83973|lt=Tiananmen|1=Tiananmen}}, in what is now {{ill|Zhongshan Park|en|Zhongshan Park|WD=Q2622640|lt=Zhongshan Park|1=Zhongshan Park}}. Originally established using a temple that had existed since the Tang dynasty, it is said to have been founded in 1420 by {{ill|Hongwu Emperor|en|Hongwu Emperor|WD=Q9957|lt=Zhu Yuanzhang|1=Hongwu Emperor}}, the founder of the Ming dynasty. The name "Zhongshan Park" derives from the fact that the casket of {{ill|Sun Yat-sen|en|Sun Yat-sen|WD=Q8573|lt=Sun Yat-sen|1=Sun Yat-sen}} (also known by his courtesy name, Zhongshan, who died in 1925), the "Father of the Chinese Revolution", is enshrined in the {{ill|Zhongshan Hall|en|Zhongshan Hall|WD=Q6145247|lt=Zhongshan Hall|1=Zhongshan Hall}} within the park. Originally, the Zhongshan Hall served as the worship hall, constructed in the Ming dynasty; it was the venue where the Ming and Qing emperors conducted ceremonies to avoid inclement weather while enshrining the deities. However, after Sun Yat-sen’s casket was interred there, the hall was renamed Zhongshan Hall in 1928, and the entire shashoku altar complex was renamed Zhongshan Park. Traditionally, the Chinese rulers were believed to receive the Mandate of Heaven here. Zhongshan Park still houses numerous ancient cypress trees, some said to be over a thousand years old, which are regarded as connecting heaven and earth. The current Chinese leader, {{ill|Xi Jinping|en|Xi Jinping|WD=Q15031|lt=Xi Jinping|1=Xi Jinping}}, who serves as General Secretary of the {{ill|General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party|en|General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party|WD=Q849418|lt=Communist Party of China|1=General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party}} and President of the {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=People's Republic of China|1=China}}, is also perceived as paying close attention to the Beijing Shashoku Altar as part of his role as China’s ruler.
== = Shashoku in Korea and North Korea == At {{ill|Gyeongbokgung|en|Gyeongbokgung|WD=Q482485|lt=Gyeongbokgung Palace|1=Gyeongbokgung}}, an ancestral temple is located on the east side and a shashoku altar ({{ill|Sashikdan|ja|社稷壇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sashikdan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) on the west side, both of which have been designated as important cultural properties in South Korea. In addition, place names such as Sashik-dong (社稷洞) and Sashik-ro (社稷路) in Seoul bear testimony to this heritage. Every year, the city of Seoul holds the [https://m.korea.net/japanese/NewsFocus/History/view?articleId=140938&page=1]{{ill|Seoul Shashoku Festival|ja|ソウル社稷大祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seoul Shashoku Festival|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Autumn Shashoku Festival).
In Chinese literature, the government of North Korea under the {{ill|Workers' Party of Korea|en|Workers' Party of Korea|WD=Q49623|lt=Workers’ Party of Korea|1=Workers' Party of Korea}} has been referred to as the “Four Carriages of the Korean Shashoku Organization.” These four carriages specifically denote the {{ill|Supreme People's Assembly|en|Supreme People's Assembly|WD=Q714698|lt=Supreme People's Assembly|1=Supreme People's Assembly}}, its {{ill|Standing Committee|ja|最高人民会議常任委員会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Standing Committee|1=Standing Committee of the Supreme People's Assembly|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11515680}}, the {{ill|State Affairs Commission|ja|国務委員会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/State Affairs Commission|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 朝鮮民主主義人民共和国国務委員会|1=State Affairs Commission of North Korea|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q25263528}} (formerly the National Defense Commission), and the {{ill|Cabinet (government)|en|Cabinet (government)|WD=Q640506|lt=Cabinet|1=Cabinet (government)}} of North Korea.
== = Shashoku in Vietnam == {{Referencesの明記| section = 1| date = 2020th year 6月}} According to {{ill|Ngô Sĩ Liên|en|Ngô Sĩ Liên|WD=Q716585|lt=Ngô Thời Lân|1=Ngô Sĩ Liên}}’s ''{{ill|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|en|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|WD=Q855899|lt=Đại Việt Sử Ký Toàn Thư|1=Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư}}'', the beginning of shashoku rituals in Vietnam can be traced back to the founding of the Hoa Lu Shashoku Altar by Ding Bùlǐng, the former emperor of the Ding dynasty of Đại Cổ Quế Quốc, in the first year of the 【Kai Bao】 era (968) during the reign of {{ill|Song Taizu|ja|宋太祖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Song Taizu|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 趙匡胤|1=Emperor Taizu of Song|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7471}}. Since the Ding dynasty, shashoku rituals in Vietnam have been regarded as major national ceremonies. During the {{ill|Nguyễn dynasty|en|Nguyễn dynasty|WD=Q6500483|lt=Nguyễn Dynasty|1=Nguyễn dynasty}}, not only was the shashoku altar established at the national level, but altars were also set up in each province alongside the {{ill|Temple of Confucius|en|Temple of Confucius|WD=Q618618|lt=Confucius Temple|1=Temple of Confucius}} (also known as the Wen or Holy Temple). These local shashoku rituals continue to be observed today, such as in the case of the "[https://btgcp.gov.vn/tin-trong-nuoc/Le_hoi_den_Xa_Tac___cot_moc_van_hoa_noi_bien_ai-postrm06axpx.html Quang Ninh Province, Mong Cai City Shashoku Festival]" (as reported by the Vietnamese Government’s Religious Affairs Division).
Regarding the national shashoku altar in Vietnam, according to records in {{ill|Lê Quý Đôn|ja|黎貴惇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lê Quý Đôn|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}’s ''{{ill|Minh Vân Tiểu Lục|ja|見聞小録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minh Vân Tiểu Lục|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'', the Shenglun Shashoku Altar (the Hanoi Shashoku Altar) was established by Lê Thánh Tông (also known as {{ill|Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja|阮世祖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}/Nguyễn Phúc Ảnh, also called Jialong Di [Zha Long Di]) during the reign of the Hong De period of the {{ill|Lê dynasty|en|Lê dynasty|WD=Q10800789|lt=Lê Dynasty|1=Lê dynasty}}. After Lê Thánh Tông’s death, a series of royal struggles and internecine conflicts ensued (Lê Dynasty → Mạc Dynasty → Lê-Mạc Wars → Zheng-Nguyễn Wars → Zheng-Xishan Wars → {{ill|Tây Sơn dynasty|en|Tây Sơn dynasty|WD=Q1034173|lt=Seoshan Dynasty|1=Tây Sơn dynasty}} → Nguyễn-Xishan Wars → {{ill|Nguyễn dynasty|en|Nguyễn dynasty|WD=Q6500483|lt=Nguyễn Dynasty|1=Nguyễn dynasty}}). The Hanoi Shashoku Altar (consisting of the sha altar and the jiki altar) was completely destroyed soon after Lê Quý Đôn’s account (after the abdication of Emperor Lê Mín, around 1788), and its original location was lost; however, in November 2006, the remains of the sha altar were discovered during road construction in Hanoi. Consequently, place names such as Phường Xã Đàn and Đường Xã Đàn have been derived from it. In addition, the "Fuh Chun Shashoku Altar" in Hue, as recorded in the first volume of the corrected edition of the ''{{ill|Đại Nam Thực Lục Chính Biên|ja|大南寔録正編|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Đại Nam Thực Lục Chính Biên|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'', was established in the fourth year of the Jia Long era (1805–1806) by Emperor {{ill|Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja|阮世祖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nguyễn Thế Tô|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Đại Nam (the Nguyễn Dynasty). Even under French colonial rule, it was not destroyed; a portion still remains in Hue City (the capital of Thừa Thiên–Huế Province) in the area known as Phường Thuận Hóa, and since 2008 the provincial government has been holding the [https://thuathienhue.gov.vn/vi-vn/Thong-tin-du-dia-chi/tid/Le-te-Xa-Tac/newsid/710FF67B-C749-4E5F-AA2D-A73F00AE0887/cid/11920A02-33B3-4D47-BBF1-EA00ED61C66D Hue Shashoku Festival] (Autumn Shashoku Festival) there. The shashoku rituals of Thừa Thiên–Huế Province, like those in Quang Ninh Province, are now recognized by the state and the Communist Party (via the Government Religious Affairs Division) as official local ceremonies.
In Vietnamese celestial charts, the portion of the zodiac corresponding to the {{ill|Scorpio (astrology)|en|Scorpio (astrology)|WD=Q134398|lt=Scorpius|1=Scorpio (astrology)}} – namely, the {{ill|Room (Chinese constellation)|en|Room (Chinese constellation)|WD=Q1145870|lt=Fangxiu|1=Room (Chinese constellation)}} (consisting of stars such as those in the π Scorpii group) – is envisioned as the crown, while the {{ill|Heart (Chinese constellation)|en|Heart (Chinese constellation)|WD=Q1145909|lt=Xin Xiu|1=Heart (Chinese constellation)}} (comprising stars such as {{ill|Antares|en|Antares|WD=Q12166|lt=Antares|1=Antares}}) is seen as a rounded back; together, these asterisms are identified with {{ill|Shennong|en|Shennong|WD=Q313336|lt=Shennong|1=Shennong}} (see [https://www.noron.vn/post/than-nong-co-phai-chom-sao-bo-cap-efsjh7gst6y Thần Nông]), and are revered as the shashoku deity (the grain deity). This Vietnamese constellation corresponds to the {{ill|Azure Dragon|ja|青龍|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Azure Dragon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 青竜|1=Azure Dragon|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q515882}} of Chinese star lore. According to the Vietnamese myth recorded in the ''{{ill|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|en|Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư|WD=Q855899|lt=Đại Việt Sử Ký Toàn Thư|1=Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư}}'', Hun Vương (the first king of the Bunlang State of the Hong family, also identified with {{ill|Kinh Dương Vương|en|Kinh Dương Vương|WD=Q1140378|lt=Jingyangwang|1=Kinh Dương Vương}}/King Jin-Son), was a descendant (or grandson in the third generation) of the first Shennong of the Flame Emperor (【Di Shinian】), and was depicted with a dragon body.
The Vietnamese revolutionary leader {{ill|Ho Chi Minh (disambiguation)|en|Ho Chi Minh (disambiguation)|WD=Q611752|lt=Ho Chi Minh|1=Ho Chi Minh (disambiguation)}} (Hu Chi Minh) had contacts with the elder {{ill|Sun Yat-sen|en|Sun Yat-sen|WD=Q8573|lt=Sun Yat-sen|1=Sun Yat-sen}} during his stay in Guangzhou (1924–1925) and revered him as a great revolutionary; however, likely due to the fact that the hall enshrining Sun Yat-sen (the {{ill|Zhongshan Hall|en|Zhongshan Hall|WD=Q6145247|lt=Zhongshan Hall|1=Zhongshan Hall}}) was located within the Beijing Shashoku Altar (the Chinese shashoku), which symbolized the Chinese state, Vietnamese people avoided using the name "Zhongshan" and instead referred to Sun Yat-sen respectfully as "Mr. Sun Wen" or "Mr. Sun Yat-sen."
